target: AG1’s claim that AI improves quality of life, health, standard of living, learning/work efficiency, accessibility, and workplace safety enough to make society better overall
objection: AI automates or augments tasks in labor markets, which can reduce demand for human work and shift economic gains away from workers, harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses through job insecurity and wage pressure.

target: AG1’s implicit claim that AI helps people think and learn better
objection: When AI supplies answers, content, or recommendations, users can outsource reasoning to the system instead of practicing independent thought, so AI undermines critical thinking skills for students and adults.

target: AG1’s implicit claim that AI benefits marginalized groups without major downsides
objection: Many AI systems are trained on data that reflects existing social inequalities and then generalize those patterns to new cases, so AI can repeat and exacerbate racism and harm racial minorities.

target: AG1’s implicit claim that AI can be broadly beneficial without serious privacy costs
objection: AI deployment often requires collecting and processing personal or sensitive user data, creating dangerous privacy risks.

target: AG2’s claim that the harms raised by AI are inevitable or unavoidable
objection: AI can improve education and workplace safety, and responsible AI practices such as privacy-preserving data handling, bias testing/mitigation, and educational uses that prompt reasoning can substantially reduce the privacy, bias, and critical-thinking concerns.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards and transition support will offset AI harms
objection: In many real deployments, substantial mitigation requires reliable upfront safeguards, but privacy-preserving handling, bias mitigation, and worker-transition support are often absent or insufficient in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms outweigh its benefits despite accessibility gains
objection: AI’s impact is use-dependent: it can generate major accessibility gains for people with disabilities even alongside risks like privacy or discrimination, and those inclusion gains matter for societal welfare.

target: AG2’s claim that harms dominate overall social impact
objection: AI can improve health and thereby raise both day-to-day quality of life and standard of living, and there is no evidence that harms like job insecurity, worsened critical thinking, racial bias, or privacy risks necessarily dominate those health gains.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves critical thinking by reducing routine load
objection: AI tools often provide ready-made answers and other outputs that users can accept rather than independently derive, so AI tends to undermine critical thinking instead of strengthening it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking
objection: AI can streamline routine work while preserving user responsibility for evaluation, so it can free attention for evidence assessment and problem-solving and thereby strengthen critical thinking instead of weakening it.

target: AG1’s claim that educational AI can foster reasoning and learning
objection: In typical educational use, students can copy complete AI-generated answers or drafts, and generative-AI systems do not require users to produce or verify step-by-step reasoning, so AI copy-paste use tends to undermine critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that AI copy-paste use is the typical or necessary educational mode
objection: Many AI outputs are presented as drafts or suggestions with evidence or uncertainty signals, and users are ordinarily expected to review and verify them; in that interactive mode, AI can engage and train critical-thinking skills rather than eliminate them.

target: AG1’s claim that AI use usually involves independent review and thus trains reasoning
objection: Many AI systems provide ready-to-paste outputs, and deadlines and performance pressures make users likely to accept them without meaningful review, so AI often fails to train independent evidence assessment.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy and discrimination are inherent or structurally unavoidable in AI deployment
objection: AI can be deployed with privacy-preserving methods such as data minimization, encryption, access controls, federated learning, and differential privacy, and with fairness testing, constrained decisions, and human oversight so that surveillance and discriminatory outcomes are not inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that mitigation meaningfully solves privacy and discrimination harms in practice
objection: In real commercial deployments, privacy-preserving measures are often not fully implemented because performance and personalization depend on large-scale data, and fairness measures are imperfect, so substantial privacy exposure and discriminatory outcomes persist despite mitigation attempts.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily increases surveillance and discriminatory profiling
objection: AI can be deployed using privacy-preserving approaches and fairness safeguards that reduce data exposure and discriminatory effects, so AI does not inherently have to increase surveillance or harm vulnerable groups.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy and fairness techniques sufficiently prevent AI harms in real deployments
objection: Even with privacy-preserving techniques and fairness auditing, real-world AI deployments often still retain substantial privacy exposure and continue to produce discriminatory outcomes because data collection remains broad and mitigation is imperfect.

target: AG2’s claim that real-world AI inevitably produces net-negative social effects
objection: AI deployments can use privacy-preserving methods and fairness measures to avoid structural surveillance and discriminatory harms while still delivering substantial benefits, so the overall impact can be positive rather than negative.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy/fairness measures make AI net-positive overall
objection: In real deployments, AI often still depends on large-scale data collection and linkage, and fairness measures do not reliably eliminate discriminatory outcomes, so the remaining harms tend to outweigh the benefits in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that AI deployment inevitably harms privacy and minorities
objection: AI can be deployed with privacy-preserving and fairness safeguards that constrain harmful behavior, making adverse privacy and discriminatory outcomes preventable rather than inevitable in relevant deployments.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards keep AI’s harms below its benefits
objection: Even when privacy and anti-discrimination safeguards exist, AI still typically requires individualized behavioral inference and monitoring, which creates ongoing privacy harms such as erosion of autonomy, reduced informed consent, and chilling effects that can make AI not good for society overall.

target: AG2’s assumption that comparable personalization benefits require individualized tracking
objection: Some AI systems can run on-device or with federated learning, data minimization, and differential privacy so they provide recommendations and personalization without continuous server-side tracking; therefore, comparable benefits can exist without individualized monitoring.
